topics.title: Living things and non-living things
topics.content:
Meaning: everything around us is either a living thing (has life) or a non-living thing (has no life). Examples of living things: goat, mango tree, mosquito, human being. Examples of non-living things: stone, water, chair, air.

Characteristics of living things (MR NIGER D):
- Movement: living things move themselves. A goat walks; a stone only moves when pushed.
- Respiration: living things breathe in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
- Nutrition: living things take in food. Plants make their own food; animals eat other things.
- Irritability: living things respond to changes around them. You blink when light suddenly shines in your eyes.
- Growth: living things grow from small to big.
- Excretion: living things remove waste from their bodies, for example sweat.
- Reproduction: living things produce young ones of their kind.
- Death: every living thing dies at some time.

Evaluation questions:
1. Mention three living things and three non-living things in your compound.
2. State five characteristics of living things.
3. Why is a motor car not a living thing even though it moves and uses fuel?

topics.title: Classification of living things
topics.content:
Scientists sort living things into groups so they can be studied easily. This is called classification.

The two big groups are plants and animals.

Animals can be grouped in several ways:
- By what they eat: herbivores eat plants (goat, cow), carnivores eat flesh (lion, hawk), omnivores eat both (man, pig).
- By where they live: land animals (antelope), water animals (fish), air and land animals (bat).
- By their body covering: mammals have hair, birds have feathers, fish have scales, reptiles have dry scales.

Plants can also be grouped:
- Flowering plants, for example mango, bean, hibiscus.
- Non-flowering plants, for example fern, moss, algae.
- By their stem: trees have woody stems, shrubs are smaller with woody stems, herbs have soft green stems.

Evaluation questions:
1. Group these animals: goat, fish, eagle, toad, cow.
2. What is the difference between a flowering and a non-flowering plant?
3. Give two examples each of herbivore, carnivore and omnivore.

topics.title: The human digestive system
topics.content:
The digestive system is the group of organs that breaks food down so the body can use it.

The parts and their work:
- Mouth: teeth grind the food and saliva (spit) starts to soften it.
- Oesophagus (gullet): a tube that pushes food down to the stomach.
- Stomach: a bag that churns food with digestive juice.
- Small intestine: food is fully broken down here and the useful parts pass into the blood. This is called absorption.
- Large intestine: water is absorbed from the leftover food.
- Anus: the solid waste (faeces) leaves the body here.

Good feeding habits: wash your hands before eating, eat balanced meals, chew food well, do not talk or run while eating, drink enough clean water.

Evaluation questions:
1. Arrange these in order: small intestine, mouth, stomach, anus, large intestine, oesophagus.
2. Where does absorption of digested food happen?
3. Mention three good feeding habits.

topics.title: Energy: meaning, sources and uses
topics.content:
Energy is the ability to do work. When you run, think, cook or light a bulb, energy is being used.

Forms of energy: chemical energy (in food and fuel), heat energy (in fire), light energy (from the sun), sound energy (from a drum), electrical energy (in a wire), kinetic energy (in moving things), potential energy (in a stretched catapult).

Sources of energy: the sun is the main source. Others are food, fuelwood, kerosene, petrol, coal, moving water (hydro power), wind and batteries.

Uses of energy: cooking food, lighting our homes, moving cars and buses, playing music, grinding pepper, keeping food cold in a fridge.

We must use energy wisely. Switch off bulbs and fans you are not using. It saves money and protects the environment.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define energy in your own words.
2. Mention four sources of energy and one use of each.
3. Why is the sun called the main source of energy?
